title: Gateless Barrier, Case 13: Te-Shan : Bowls in Hand
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching is about embracing the impermanence and uncertainty of life, letting go of our need for control and explanations, and approaching spiritual practice with a sense of curiosity and openness. By accepting what is happening in the present moment, without judgment or attachment to fixed views, we can cultivate a deeper sense of humility, emptiness, and compassion. This allows us to approach life's challenges with greater ease and wisdom, trusting in the natural flow of time and the unfolding of our own spiritual journey.

sentences.text: Isn't our stuff funny?
You're supposed to face this way, not that way.
There's a complex little way that the person is supposed to hand me a lectern, which I never ever told her before, but somehow I thought she would know.
So we create this whole ridiculous situation together so we can learn, right?
So we can learn something, we hope.
And it's this whole situation that we call sesshin, just two Chinese characters.
It stands for something really big.
On the one hand, it's really lovely, peaceful.
What a way to get to live for a week: to be quiet, really pay attention to what we're doing, and just have so much room for things that we forget to leave room for, like looking up at the sky.
Yesterday morning I was walking along, and I noticed I was hunched forward a little bit, and feeling a little bit rushed.
I had made a big deal with the other organizers about showing up on time, so I was receiving karmic retribution for that.
But then something caught my eye up above, and I just happened to look up, and I just stopped for a moment in awe of the dawn sky, the clouds, lumpy, gray.
Gray to white, washed with pink.
And I thought, wow, how lucky we are to have eyes in the sky.
And how lucky we are to have this week, where once in a while we remember how lucky we are to be freed from so many of the trappings of our busy lives.
If you're following the guidelines, and I hope you are, free from so many things, right?
Emails and texts and all the whatevers.

And then I was realizing, free from this complex calculus we're constantly doing about whom to answer on what medium and how frequently and in what way, so that it will all work out the best and they will still like us and we will get our work done.
Oh my gosh, we're so used to this, it's normal, but it's also exhausting even to think about it.
So we're free from so much.
And how wonderful to be fed delicious food three times a day.
No shopping, no cooking, no going out and feeling vaguely guilty for not shopping and cooking.
Free from all kinds of decisions about what to do and when and how much.
We can just follow the schedule.
We just breathe, we walk, we stand, we sit, we lie down.
And somehow this design enables 60 people, there's 60 people in this room, to do this together in relative harmony.
That's pretty amazing.
And you could probably tell I was doing a set it up and knock it down oratorial trick there.
Just like Buddha, I learned it from the best.
This guy over here does that a lot, have you noticed that?
How difficult this is, too.
So many complicated rituals, for one thing.
It was a common topic in the Dokusan room: "I thought this was about, like, freedom or something.
What's with all these rituals?"
And as if what we were already doing wasn't enough, this year we had a go in [unclear: "Adoryoki"].
And I think we can all agree with Norman that it's the most wonderful way to eat a meal.
It's also the world's most complicated way to eat a meal at the same time.
And the thing I want to especially keep in mind, and encourage all of us who've been at this a while to keep in mind, is that there's also a lot of insider knowledge going on.
It's easy for us to forget this.
So many of us have internalized all kinds of little details, and we accidentally shame and embarrass other people just by doing our thing, making them feel like they don't know what's going on.
So we're sorry about that.
We don't mean to.
And there are so many examples of this.
One I noticed is, suppose you're sitting there at the table, having somehow gotten through this complicated meal ritual, and somebody holds out a stack of little chant cards without saying anything.
Are you supposed to put your card on that stack?
Are you supposed to take the stack and put yours on it?
And if so, then what are you supposed to do with it?
Are you supposed to keep it?
Are you supposed to pass it this way, pass it that way?
What are you supposed to do with this stack of cards?
You're just trying to get through the meal and they're giving you things.
There's no explanation.
It's really difficult.
And then you're surrounded by people.
And I'm sure they're wonderful people and everything.
Very sincere.
But they can be a bit much.
Funny little things they do or don't do.
They're either following the rules way too assiduously, so prideful, or they're slacking off.
Nobody quite gets it right.
That form was announced very clearly yesterday.
Why didn't she do it right?
Oh, I bet she came late to the meeting.
And the organizers, oh my gosh.
I mean, they're pretty good in everything.
But they really should have, fill in the blank.
We all have something to fill in that blank.
We should have something to make this work better.
It's obvious.
It's obvious.
Very sneaky of them to put that guideline in about not giving them feedback until later, too.
It's clever.
Protection.
So I'll write my note now while I'm thinking about it.
And I'll post it on the last morning.
Straighten that out.
And then either it'll be better thanks to me, or I'll be righteously indignant that they didn't follow my suggestion.
And of course it's both, isn't it?
It's really both wonderful and difficult to do this together for a week.
I think the thing that always amazes me and will never stop amazing me is that we would never have thought of this.
But somehow we received some version of this.
Admittedly we have tweaked it, but we wouldn't have even had a thing to tweak.
We never would have thought of living this way for a week as being beneficial.
But as we watch each other over the years and decades, we see, we don't know why exactly, but we see how beneficial it is.
The way we're all getting, little by little with zigs and zags, a little bit wiser, a little bit kinder, a little softer maybe.
But able to step up when we need to step up.
And although we do know we're very privileged to be here, to have this opportunity, sometimes maybe we get caught in a really bad mood and we forget that we're privileged, but it comes back.
So although that's true, we're privileged, we also see over time that we're not doing this for us or it never would have worked anyway.
We're doing this for all the people that we love.
And gradually as we practice, that circle of love gets bigger and bigger and we realize we're doing this for everybody without exception.
Even the ones that really creep us out.
Even them.
We're doing this for them.
I won't name names.
And of course in the center, seemingly in the center of all this, is our practice of zazen.
And I was thinking of a saying from a Zen Center teacher, San Francisco Zen Center teacher, Paul Haller.
I've not heard him say this.
I've not spent much time with Paul, but it's been reported that he has this great saying, which I assume he says during zazen, somewhere in the middle when we're all kind of twisted up in knots.
The saying is, "There's nothing happening that shouldn't be happening.
And there's nothing that isn't happening that should be happening."
Interesting turn of phrase.
There's nothing happening that should not be happening.
And there's nothing that's not happening that should be happening.
And I think we sit down for a while and we see that that's really true.
That's how it is.
It couldn't really be any other way.
Things arise in the mind according to conditions.

Not that we can always see or understand those conditions, no matter how hard we try, but we have this sense over time, like, wow, this is just what's arising, what's happening according to something.
Something bigger than me.
Here it is.
Good thought, bad thought, maybe a little moment of no thought, non-thought.
It's all coming and going as it does.

There's some sense of a witness that I call me watching this, maybe giving a little more juice to the ones I like, or maybe giving a little more juice to the ones I don't like, counter-productively causing suffering.
Every time you see this whole thing happening, thoughts, emotions come and go, twinges in the body come and go, sometimes very sharp and strong moments, sometimes acres of dullness, sleepiness.
I can't tell you how many times in the Dokusan room, this is probably true in Dokusan rooms everywhere, that someone has come and said, "All right, what is the solution to sleepiness?"
And they're so freaked out when I say, "No solution, accept it," or relieved, maybe: "Oh, really?
I don't have to fight that anymore?
It's just what happens?"
There's nothing that is happening that should not be happening.
Does it actually include sleeping?
Isn't that a sin or something?
There's a little essay I like about meditation in which he says, "You have permission to go to sleep in meditation.
How else will you ever know waking up if you don't give yourself permission to go to sleep?"
And that there's nothing that isn't happening that should be happening: we act as if there's something else that should be happening.
But it is kind of axiomatic that that does not make sense, if you think about it.
Because the only things that aren't happening that could or should or might be happening are things which you are imagining should be happening.
So this is absolutely your imagination.
It's inherently a fantasy.
And we're good at that.
We can think and imagine all kinds of states and experiences and realizations and moments like we heard about or read about or imagined.
It's exactly just thinking and imagining.
No different from any other thought.
Do we think we can predict the future?
A little bit of neuroscience, I think I know, points here to an interesting thing.

So it turns out that the same areas of the cortex that are involved in doing an actual thing, like actually perceiving something that's real, so-called real, the same areas are involved in imagining the same kind of experience.
So like seeing an actual apple in the dining room, or a chopped up pile of apples in your bowl, there's this complex thing that happens that Buddhist psychology and Western science try to explain.
You perceive an apple.

And then there's this chain of neural events that happen in your visual cortex, an area of the brain kind of in the back, with all kinds of neurons firing and stuff happening, and there's describable stages, there's level one, two, three, four, apparently, as you perceive a visual object.

We zoom way down, there's these little neurons, these long, stretched out cells that have these electrical potentials that cause these neurotransmitters to squirt out chemicals, other neurons receive those chemicals, and stuff happens.
Well, it turns out, yeah, all that happens is just the same if you imagine an apple.
If you imagine an apple, your brain seems to respond in much the same way.
If there's any actual neuroscientists in here, I apologize, I'm sure that's really simplistic.
It's really trippy to think about that.
All this stuff we're worried about, what if it's just a bunch of little zaps and squirts?

A lot of them, admittedly, if there are, in fact, as they tell me, a hundred billion neurons in our head interacting in incredibly complex ways, but could our experience and our consciousness really just be an emergence of squirts and zaps?
Who knows?
But it all seems real to us, which is the point.
And since it seems real to us, it's important.

So we pay attention and practice and watch the way the mind tilts in so many funny ways when we don't accept that there's nothing here that should and that there's nothing that isn't here that should be here.
Because all of us, this points to these wonderful teachings on emptiness that Norman was reminding us about yesterday when he spoke about the meal ritual with such enthusiasm.

All these things that seem so important to us, so full of meaning and a sort of quality of solidity, that this is what it is, whether it's a concept or a dream or a physical object, it seems to our perceiving mind and heart to be so real and solid.
And to say that everything is empty is not to say that it's exactly not there, but that it's empty of something that we're pouring into it.
Empty of this quality of fixness and solidity and weight.
It's something that the great goddess Prajnaparamita is brave enough to not turn away from.
And that's liberating, the text and teachings tell us, and we can experience.
To not turn away from the reality that although it's not that there's not that important concept, it's not the way you think it is.
It's not so fixed, it's not so predictable, it's not so real.
It's only your view of it, and your view may shift and change as you change, and it's hard to let that into our hearts.
Even though they're telling us over and over again and we're having little glimpses of something that's in this territory.
Something about letting go, softening up, not being so caught and hooked.
It's hard to let that in because it's what we've been doing.
It's what we've been creating for all the years of our lives.
As we've been educated and as we've educated ourselves, we've generated a kind of internal landscape with waypoints and landmarks so that we can find our way around.
And we need that.
We need landmarks to orient.
To know who we are, to know what's going on, what the world is like.
So we can walk across the desert sighting that distant peak ahead of us and the mountains behind us and to the side of us.
As we start to tune in using this metaphor, we notice that the mountains are pretty steep and pretty much holding us in this little teeny channel, though.
The path, although clear, is limited.
But it helped us get to where we are, so we can be grateful for our confusion and our misunderstanding.
We're here because we've somehow intuited or slammed into the limits of our belief in the non-emptiness of everything, the fixness of everything.
So these teachings on emptiness are not to say, "Whoops, that's all baloney, forget about all that."
That would probably lead to some kind of big breakdown.
But actually to say, "Well, no, it's real enough, but it's like a mirage."
If you look at it carefully, you can watch it shimmer a little bit.
And that limitation, that gate without a barrier in front of you, if you just relax completely, you can walk right through it.
These mirages were needed, and probably are needed still, to help us navigate, but they're just mirages.
They're a construction of our mind, our culture, our society, our collective attempt to make some kind of sense of things.
It's built on the assumption that there is such a thing as sense in a certain way.
So these wisdom emptiness teachings are an invitation to step off of this narrow path into the Buddha lands of a bigger life.
Bigger life.
Using them when they're helpful and letting them go when they're not helpful.
All our beliefs and views, holding them all as tools for compassion.
Zazen is a great place for us to sit and study this, because there's not so much else going on.
But the wonderful thing about sesshin is that it encourages us to see the non-difference between Zazen and everything else we're doing.
That's part of what Norman, I thought, was saying about the meal: to understand the meal is also emptiness, is also Zazen practice.
Rich and wondrous and unknowable.
Delightful.
Difficult.
The whole works.
At first it may seem like Zazen is the only thing, and then we're just keeping ourselves fed and exercised and able to come back and survive three more rounds.
Then reset and come back and survive again.
I don't know what we think this is, a marathon running stages or something, with rest breaks.
Zazen is the only special time where we set aside all these burdens of limited views or ideas of right and wrong, what should and shouldn't be.
And in fact Dogen seems to imply that in the Fukanzazengi, where he says:
*When you sit down, cast aside all involvements, cease all affairs.
Do not think good or bad.
Do not administer pros and cons.
Cease all the movements of the conscious mind and the gauging of all thoughts and views.*
It's good advice.
When you sit down you should definitely do that.
You could not do that, but luckily suffering will keep reminding you relentlessly until you cut it out.
But what about when you get up?
Is he saying that when you get up, involve yourself in all affairs, think nothing but good and bad, administer nothing but pros and cons, accelerate the movements of the conscious mind?
I don't think he's suggesting that either, although we need to attend to affairs for sure.
There's a contemporary definition of mindfulness, and here by mindfulness they mean this whole process of practice, not just the Buddhist mental factor.
There's a definition I like that speaks to this elegantly, I think.
It was written by a couple of researchers who are also meditators, which is a whole fun movement of contemplative researchers.
They do the internal lab on the cushion and then they go to the physical lab.
Anyway, this is Linda Carlson and Shana Shapiro, writing:
*Mindfulness is the awareness that arises out of paying attention on purpose in an open, kind and discerning way.*
*Mindfulness is the awareness that arises out of paying attention on purpose in an open, kind and discerning way.*
Or we could say practice allows an awareness that arises from this paying attention purposefully in an open, kind and discerning way.
So that's kind of lovely, I think.
Open and kind.
Doesn't it just make you relax to hear those words, open and kind?
Oh yeah.
Yes please.
But also discerning.
Discerning is an intelligence.
Discernment.
So here, a deep discernment.
What's the feeling of this moment?
What's actually going on?
And over time this discernment attains a sort of flavor, so that we know it's really helpful discernment.
This is the flavor of emptiness.
The flavor of letting go.
The flavor of bigger than self.
This flavoring really helps us, and we feel it in our gut, where it turns out there are 100 billion neurons.
There's 100 billion neurons in your gut.
So you've got some intelligence there too, even in this physical way.
So, feeling in your gut that things are bigger, broader, softer, more fluid, more mysterious than your clever brain can put words to.
That seems to naturally support our humility.
Humility is not self-deprecation.
It's not putting ourselves down.
We need our intelligence and our skill.
We need to operate in the world that apparently is full of all these forms, and we need everything, because we need tools to work in this world as bodhisattvas and help.
But with humility we can feel that the tip of our screwdriver or the pounding surface on our hammer is empty.
We don't exactly know for sure what it is.
We know it may be useful, but we're not so sure.
So we're not so quick to assume, and we get a lot more curious, I think, and a lot more willing to ask.
Ask our heart.
Ask the others.
"Excuse me, are you a nail?
Oh, you're not a nail?
Okay, sorry.
Put this hammer down here.
I assumed you were.
Oh, you are a nail?
All right.
I can help.
Whack."
But so often our humility and our discernment helps us to see that the best thing we can do is give each other space and trust and love.
We don't need those tools just now.
We can put them back in the toolbox.
And there I think our silence practice in sesshin is such a great help.
Our silence practice is giving each other such a deep, compassionate gift, the gift of space.
Allowing each other to find our own way, to discover for ourselves the dimensions of whatever this is.
If emptiness isn't a word that works for you, use another word.
Just words, anyway.
We're all here together, but we're each of us in our own universe together.
We know that the universe is changing and developing and shifting in all kinds of ways, ways we can never really quite understand.
But when we interrupt that process for someone else, even with a really well-meaning check-in, you know, "You're okay, you're right?", somebody looks miserable, naturally we want to check in.
Maybe that's not that helpful, though.
Maybe it might even be a little bit harmful.
Harmful sounds a bit dramatic.
It may not so much be harm as a kind of dampening and limiting of the possibility of practice.
This is hard for us to really have faith in, but I think we've seen enough examples of it in our tradition to really trust that this is actually true.
It's a deeply compassionate gift to yourself and everyone else in the practice, and probably in your whole life outside of sesshin.
That's the next step, right?
If sesshin helps us go beyond Zazen to our life at Samish Island Camp, so protected, then maybe sesshin is an encouragement to understand this in everyday life too.
Of course there are times when it really helps somebody to check in with them, for sure.
But in this carefully designed situation, I think it's really good to trust the silence a little more deeply.
We're doing great and we can always go further, always deeper, which is what's wonderful in the drag about this thing.
We're never going to do it right, you know that, right?
We're never going to do this right.
But luckily, we can't do it wrong either.
So with the silence, just to tread so lightly and to trust the container, trust the leaders and the teachers and the availability of support.
It's pretty easy to get into dokusan here, pretty quick.
If someone seems miserable, they may be exactly the miserable they need to be right now.
It's hard to witness, isn't it?
Maybe out of habit we offer a little touch, a little word of encouragement.
"Maybe you should take a period off."
Maybe that's exactly the wrong thing to do, and that person needs to go through something.
And now you're making them present to you.
Or maybe it's your own suffering that's moving you, and that can be very subtle, very tricky.
So don't make more suffering.
Be kind to yourself about this.
But maybe you're just too hard to see your friend looking down.
You want to alleviate that suffering because you don't want to feel it.
So there's such deep possibilities here in the interpersonal realm, even as we're practicing on our own.
So, I seem to have picked up the bad habit of making a very long preamble to what I was going to say.
Where did I get that?
I have this little project I'm trying to follow through on, and thank you for being my captive audience.
I'll try to be brief, so you're not here forever.
And feel free, of course, to change your position, whatever you need.
It's up to you.
Maybe the pain in your knees is exactly the right pain in your knees, though.
Don't move.
I'll try to talk for many more hours.
Anyway.
Next story in the Mumonkan.
This is case 13, TeShan carrying his bowls.
*One day, TeShan went towards the dining room, carrying his bowls.
The tenzo, Juefeng, met him and asked, "The [unclear: "bow is not wrong"].
The drum has not been struck.
Where are you going, teacher, carrying your bowls?"
TeShan turned and went back to his room.
Later, Juefeng mentioned this to the head monk, Yanto.
And Yanto said, "TeShan is great, but he does not understand the last word."
TeShan, the teacher, heard about this remark and sent his attendant to get Yanto.
"You do not approve of me?" he demanded.
And then Yanto whispered something in the master's ear.
And TeShan was relieved.
The next day, TeShan ascended the teaching seat and gave a Dharma talk that was very different from before.
And Yanto, going forward to the front of the hall, clapped his hands and laughed out loud, saying, "Great joy, our old master has understood the last word.
From now on, nobody in the whole country can check him, can equal him."*
So interestingly, after we just talked all about the meal, we have a story that starts about the meal.
The teacher is carrying his Oryoki set down to the meal.
Like here, they don't leave the sets sitting on the table, you bring your bowls.

Or maybe more likely, the monks are living in a monk's hall, which is the genius, crazy invention of Zen that maybe most of us will never experience, but someone should go check it out and tell us how it is.
The idea is that you live in this room, and you have a little space, one tatami mat space, where you sit, sleep, and eat.
In the back is a little cupboard in which you're allowed to have like five things, no personal stuff.
Your bowls, your futon, your covers, maybe you get to change underwear, I don't know.
So it would all happen right in the room.
You just reach behind, you open your cupboard, get your bowls out, [unclear: "sitting in zaz in it"].
But the teacher would live in the teacher's room, which is up at the top of the monastery, symbolically the very top of the place.
So maybe he was walking to the monk's hall with his bowls.
But the monks were not ready to eat.
Why is he here?
The [unclear: "umpam"] bell hasn't been rung, and the meal drum hasn't begun.
So why did he do that?
Did the teacher just get mixed up?
Some versions of the story say the meal was late, and he just went down at the usual time.
And isn't it great we have such clear signals?
Do you notice that?
There's signals for everything.
One of the great potentials for sesshin is you could take your watch off.
We forgot to mention that in the orientation, I think.
You don't have to wear a watch, I don't think.
If you're finding you can follow along, okay, leave your watch in your room.
Turn off that phone, which you definitely only have airplane mode to check the time on.
And just trust the signals.
Not because watches are bad, but it may be an interesting way to explore your relationship to time.
So I think our relationship to time is not always that healthy, right?
We're a bit harried by time.
I don't have enough time, don't waste time, and so on.
And the clock creates a sort of linear version of time, which maybe we could let go of and see what happens.
So anyway, maybe TeShan in the story was relating to time in a certain way.
Or maybe the meal was late, we don't know.
And then there's these two students who interact with the teacher and interact with each other.
We know from other stories that these two students are Dharma brothers, Xue Feng and Yan Tou.
So another thing we'll never get right is pronouncing the Chinese.
And we know from other stories that Xue Feng, the first guy, the Tenzo, is like one of these wonderful Zen characters who's really earnest, trying so hard, but doesn't get it.
I love that character, because I am that character.
Maybe you are too.
And the other student, Yan Tou, is the composed, realized being who just hangs out in emptiness and always knows the right thing to say or do.
These stories select a little bit for those two characters.
The stories where Yan Tou blows it don't make the canon.
The most famous story about these two is worth mentioning.
Let's see.
Oh, where'd it go?
Excuse me.
Yeah, here it is.
Oh, couldn't open that page.
Siri doesn't want that one.
Anyway, I'll just say it briefly because I'm running late.
One time the two Dharma brothers, Xue Feng and Yan Tou, are walking from one monastery to the other in the winter and a terrible snowstorm starts up.
So they have to take refuge in an inn.
But Xue Feng, who is so earnest and doesn't get it, says, "Oh, okay.
We're stuck here.
I'll just sit zazen day and night."
Obviously, that'd be the thing to do.
And Yan Tou just snoozes.
And eventually Deishan gets, I mean, Xue Feng, I'm sorry, the earnest one gets a little pissed off.
"Why are you just snoozing?"
And Yan Tou says some clever thing about, "Oh, you think you can get something out of all that you're doing."
So that's the story that's going on there.
It reminds us of the other famous story.
There are so many stories about this, and they're really relevant to what we're trying to do this week.
What do we think we're trying to do?
What do we think we're going to get?
The other story has the monk sitting there doing night sitting, which we encourage.
We haven't mentioned it yet.
Sorry to mention it now.
After 9 o'clock, you could go brush your teeth and you could actually come back here.
It could be for long, don't worry.
You don't have to be like Xue Feng.
But the student was sitting up late, very earnest, and the teacher wanders by and picks up a broken tile from the ground they were renovating or something.
He gets out his handkerchief and starts rubbing the tile vigorously.
Same thing: eventually the earnest monk gets pissed off and says something, very politely, to the teacher.
"Excuse me, honored teacher, why are you doing that?"
And the teacher says, "Oh, I'm making a mirror.
I'm polishing this up.
I'm going to make a nice mirror."
The student says, "You can't make a mirror out of polishing a tile!"
The teacher says, "Yep.
And you can't make a Buddha by sitting zazen like that."
I want to briefly apologize for all these stories.
Yep, they're all men.
So just know that we notice that.
Once in a while we forget, but we notice that.
And we try to bring up stories about women as well, which are so wonderful and more and more becoming available.
But this is such a core part of our tradition, it's worth meeting these guys.
They're trying their best.
But they're a part of the culture they were in, as we are now, so sorry about that.
Anyway, let's finish the story before your knees explode.
So Jue Feng mentions this funny little encounter to his Dharma brother, Yanto.
"Funniest thing happened.
The teacher came down at the wrong time.
I told him it's not time for the meal, and he just left.
What do you make of that?"
And Yanto replies in a way that's supposed to shake his friend up a little bit, to make him see that there are some deeper possibilities here.
There may have been a real deep teaching in the way Deshan responded to this correction.
The student said, "You're here at the wrong time?"
Back to his room.
So, in the story, Yanto replies, "Ah, Deshan is great, but he did not understand the last word."
You're supposed to freak out Jue Feng a little bit.
He's great, but he doesn't understand the last word.
What?
And then they go off, and in these stories the monk always goes off and thinks about it for quite a while.
It would be rude to ask your Dharma brother, "What do you mean by that?
What are you talking about?"
Or maybe your Dharma brother wouldn't respond anyway.
And Deshan, the abbot, heard about this little exchange and what Yanto said, and summoned him to his room at the top of the monastery and asked him about this.
And Yanto, in response, whispers in his teacher's ear.
And Deshan is happy.
He's relieved.
You've probably heard of the wonderful and intense way our Rinzai brothers and sisters work with these koans.
The teacher assigns you some key phrase to sit with day or night.
I have not studied this one in that way, but I believe from the commentaries I've read by such teachers that this whispering in the ear is maybe one of those key phrases.
What did the teacher whisper?
You can sit with that.
What did he whisper?
The idea is you just get so intimate with that moment, like you were inside Deshan's ear somehow, a little teeny person.
